---
# HOW THIS FILE IS LAID OUT
#
# Each slide is a "## Heading", one drawing, and its speaker notes.
#
# Every slide is a sheet of ruled paper. The drawings are plain SVG inside
# ```{=html} fences, in a 1124 x 480 box where one unit is one pixel on the
# slide and the page's rules fall on y = 0, 32, 64 ... 480. Handwriting is given
# a y on (or a pixel above) one of those, so it sits on the line.
#
#   data-r                        a line to be redrawn as a pen stroke (Rough.js)
#   <use href="#ph-name">         a photograph from img/ (make-photo-parts.mjs)
#   class="cut"                   ...cut out and stuck down
#   class="zoom" data-zoom="..."  ...that can be clicked to look at it larger
#   <g class="patch" data-over="#id">   correction fluid over that word
#   <text class="pen" data-patch="id">  what gets written on that patch
#
# The speaker notes are the ::: {.notes} blocks. They are ordinary Markdown and
# are the part most worth editing.
#
# (Nothing may come between this header and the first "##": anything that does
# becomes a blank slide of its own.)
pagetitle: "Painting Over the Mistake — White-Out as an Educational Technology"
author: "Jeremy Sheeshka"
date: "October 2026"
lang: en-CA
format:
  revealjs:
    theme: default
    css: whiteout.css
    # photo-parts.include.html is generated (make-photo-parts.mjs, run by
    # render.sh); the other two are written by hand. The script runs last.
    include-after-body:
      - photo-parts.include.html
      - deck-parts.include.html
      - deck-script.include.html
    embed-resources: true
    # There is no math in the deck. Without this, reveal's math plugin fetches
    # MathJax from a CDN on every visit — the only thing the file would not
    # already contain.
    html-math-method: plain
    width: 1280
    height: 720
    margin: 0
    center: false
    auto-stretch: false
    controls: true
    controls-layout: bottom-right
    controls-tutorial: false
    progress: true
    # The assignment is five slides. The cover and the reference list are not
    # two of them, so reveal's own "3 / 7" counter would say the wrong thing.
    # Each counted slide carries "n of 5" in its top margin instead.
    slide-number: false
    menu: false
    hash: true
    history: false
    navigation-mode: linear
    # The page turn is in whiteout.css; reveal's own transitions are off.
    transition: none
    background-transition: none
    pdf-separate-fragments: false
---

::: {.notes}
For this presentation I am looking at white-out (correction fluid) as an educational technology.

The title has a typo in it on purpose. *(Click.)* The typo gets painted over, and once the patch has dried the fix gets written on top of it in pen. The typo was never deleted, though. It is still in the file underneath the patch, and this is what the rest of the slides build on: the placement of white-out is surface level, where the writing still exists underneath and is just hidden.

*(The cover and the reference list are not counted in the five slides. The comics and the photo of the page can be clicked to see them larger.)*

## White-Out through McLuhan's tetrad {.tetrad data-kicker="1 of 5 · Media ecology" data-where="1 of 5"}

```

::: {.notes}
White-out comes out of the typewriter office before it ever shows up in a classroom. Bette Nesmith Graham worked in Dallas as a secretary and a freelance artist, and in 1954 she "stopped erasing typing errors and began using tempera paint to cover them" (Jones, 2025). Two years later she was sharing it with other secretaries as Mistake Out, and by 1958 it had been renamed Liquid Paper.

From the office it made its way into pencil cases, which is where I see it becoming a learning tool. In 2008 it was banned from schools in Seychelles, where students had been using it on their mistakes and on the furniture ("Correction Fluid Banned in Schools," 2008), and today a candidate is not allowed to use it in a Cambridge English exam (Cambridge English, n.d.). So the users I follow here are typists, students, teachers, examiners and, at the end, a cartoonist.

I put the four parts of the tetrad up at once, the way McLuhan and McLuhan (1988) print theirs (p. 129), since it "presents not a sequential process, but rather four simultaneous ones" (p. 99). White-out **enhances** a clean page that you fixed yourself, in private. It **obsolesces** the typing eraser and retyping the whole page. It **retrieves** the painter's way of fixing things, which is to paint over it (retrieval needs "some translation or metamorphosis" (p. 101), and here a studio habit comes back as an office supply). Pushed to its limit it **reverses into** a cover-up, where a patch put on too thick cracks and flakes and is the first thing you see, which is where it ends up banned on exams and forms.

The line along the bottom is where it sits in time, with the eraser and the retyped page before it, then IBM's correcting Selectric in 1973, which lifted the mistake off of the page with sticky tape (IBM, n.d.), then correction tape, and then the undo button. I see white-out as a little artifact of the space between the typewriter and digital text. There is less of a need for its original purpose now, but it still serves me.
:::

<p class="cite-line">After Latour (1992): two columns that make “a scale where tiny efforts balance out mighty weights” (p. 229); delegates as “lieutenants … holding the place of, for, someone else” (p. 239); the notice on the door, “The Groom Is On Strike” (p. 227). Photographs, cut out: 8joKeaton (2021).</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Latour (1992) has a simple way of working out what a nonhuman does, which is to "imagine what other humans or other nonhumans would have to do were this character not present" (p. 229). He has the reader put the work people would have to do without a door in one column and the "gentle pushing" in the other, and calls the result "a scale where tiny efforts balance out mighty weights" (p. 229), so I drew the scale.

On the left is the bottle (dab, wait, write over it), and on the right is the work it stands in for: the typist retypes the page, the student copies it out again, and the teacher finds the mistake and marks it. Latour's word for handing work over like this is delegation, and he calls the stand-ins "lieutenants", from the French for "holding the place of, for, someone else" (p. 239).

The question for me is which job got handed over. The bottle doesn't erase anything (the mistake is still on the page underneath the paint), so what we delegated was the hiding, and it is now the student who decides what the teacher gets to see. When correction fluid was banned in schools in Seychelles, one of the reasons given was that crossing out instead "allows teachers to see what kind of errors students are making and address them accordingly" ("Correction Fluid Banned in Schools," 2008). The student gets a clean page out of this, and the teacher loses what those mistakes would have told them.

*(Click.)* Delegates can also fail. Latour's door starts with a notice that reads "The Groom Is On Strike, For God's Sake, Keep The Door Closed" (p. 227), and a bottle of white-out does the same thing when it dries out and becomes useless, at which point all of the work on the right comes back.
:::

::: {.notes}
If delegation is the work we hand over, prescription is what comes back to us. Latour (1992) defines it as "the behavior imposed back onto the human by nonhuman delegates" (p. 232), and says you can hear it by putting the machine's silence into sentences, usually in the imperative: "do this, do that, behave this way" (p. 232). The bottle's sentences would be shake me, one thin coat, now wait.

Waiting for it to dry is like having to reflect on your mistake for a few seconds, and I built that into this slide. *(Click once to paint over "was", and click again to write on it.)* If you write on the patch before it has dried, the pen drags through it and smudges, and you have to go back and do it properly. Latour's version is the door with the strong spring where, if you aren't quick, "your nose will get shorter and bloody" (p. 232). Correction tape goes on dry and the undo button has no wait at all, so both of those take the pause away.

The assignment asks what Latour means by "what defines our social relations is, for the most part, prescribed back to us by nonhumans" (Johnson [Latour], 1988, p. 310). I take it to mean that once we have handed our jobs over to things, the things start setting the terms for how we deal with each other. My example is on the right. The ad promises "If it's written, you can take it back" (Giovanni+Draftfcb, 2012), which is white-out being used to hide something and not just to correct a mistake. An exam board says the opposite, "You are not allowed to use correction fluid, correction tape, or erasable pen", partly because the fluid "can cause issues when scanning" (Cambridge English, n.d.). So what a candidate is allowed to do with their own mistake ends up being settled between a bottle and a scanner. I suppose the expectation of a clean page, where the fix is invisible instead of going with the mistake, is something the bottle hands back to us as well.
:::

::: {.notes}
As an object, white-out is easy to describe: it is a small bottle of white fluid for covering mistakes. Latour (2005) calls that kind of description a matter of fact, and he thinks that for too long "objects have been wrongly portrayed as matters-of-fact" (p. 9).

*(Click.)* His other word is thing. The old word Thing (or Ding) was first the name for a kind of assembly (p. 12), and for centuries it meant "the issue that brings people together because it divides them" (p. 13). In his words, objects become things "when matters of fact give way to their complicated entanglements and become matters of concern" (p. 31). I painted over the typed words on purpose here, so "object" and "fact" are still under there.

This is the assembly that the bottle has gathered, and I gave seats to nonhumans as well, since Latour wants a politics that "is no longer limited to humans" (p. 31). The student wants a clean page. The teacher needs to see the mistakes, and students were using it "to write or draw on the furniture", which were both reasons given for the Seychelles ban ("Correction Fluid Banned in Schools," 2008). The exam scanner can't read through a patch (Cambridge English, n.d.). A 1985 report of four sudden deaths in adolescents who had been sniffing it asked for school health officials to be alerted, and one of the solvents in most of those fluids was later phased out worldwide because it depletes the ozone layer (King et al., 1985; Environment and Climate Change Canada, 2025). The cartoonist only needs it not to show in print, which is the next slide.

None of these parties agree on what the bottle is for, and that is what makes it a thing for me. It also won't hold still, since it comes as tape and pens now, and it has been called Mistake Out, Liquid Paper, Wite-Out or Tipp-Ex depending on who made it.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the original art for a *Drabble* comic strip from June 19, 1989. Kevin Fagan, who draws the strip, posted a photo of the original 35 years later and wrote "This original made me smile (in spite of all the Wite-Out)!" (Fagan, 2024). The detail shows it brushed on above the wishing well, and to my eye something was drawn there first and then painted out, where you can still see the outline of it. It was hidden, but it wasn't erased.

Media ecology would ask about the environment the page was made for. This board was made to be photographed and printed in newspapers, and I take it the Wite-Out is there so that the change wouldn't show in print, which means it only shows now, on a screen. McLuhan and McLuhan (1988) write that "Nothing is as stale as yesterday's newspaper - until it can be retrieved as valuable documentary evidence or nostalgic treat" (p. 100), and a post of old originals is that kind of retrieval.

ANT would ask who is doing the work, and the network I picture here is Fagan, a pen, a bottle holding the place of redrawing the whole panel, the camera that shot the board for the newspapers, the syndicate and a reader who never knew. Latour (1992) says that most of what a delegate seems to do "depends on lines of other setups being aligned" (p. 240), which is to say that if you put an exam scanner where that camera was, the same patch becomes a problem.

Where I see the two connecting is that neither one treats the bottle as a neutral tool. In tetrad form the artefact is "not neutral or passive, but an active logos or utterance" (McLuhan & McLuhan, 1988, p. 99). Where they disconnect is in what the bottle is to us: for McLuhan it is an extension "of the physical human body or the mind" (p. 93), while for Latour it is somebody else, a stand-in that can go on strike. They also differ in method, since McLuhan finds the same "four-part logos-structure" in every artefact (p. 127) while Latour says "for the analysis of artifacts we do not have a structure" (1992, p. 250).

Each of them also conceals something, a bit like the white-out does. The tetrad shows me the long arc from the typewriter to undo but paints over Fagan's own hand, while ANT shows me that hand and paints over the arc. I suppose I needed both of them to see this page properly, the same way it took a phone camera to see the Wite-Out.
:::
